doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Does race matter: segregated radio and a rainbow soul band
summary: Asked whether race matters, he describes segregated radio and playing sax in a multiethnic soul band at dances, learning that music is functional.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’m reminded that, getting back to jazz now, recently I received a DownBeat and the title in bold letters was jazz — sorry, “Race Matters.” And I said, wow, and I went over to my bookshelf, because I had saved this other issue from ten years ago from another jazz magazine, and I pulled it out and it was Nat Hentoff and the title was “Race Matters.” And so I guess my obvious question was does race matter?
Okay. How does it matter in your eyes?

How does it matter in my eyes? Well that’s too big a question to answer, God, how do you even begin? See since I was very young I loved black music. There were — radio was entirely segregated. There were white stations and black stations. The black ones were KDIA and KSOL. And I started listening to that. It was a revelation. It wasn’t something that most people in my circle would have ever listened to. I was asked to join a sort of rainbow soul band with — to be the saxophonist in a group that was Korean, Chinese, Mexican and African-American, and an Irish organist. It was a great cultural experience. I’m scared in something as sort of off the top of my head situation as a video interview to really answer that except in an anecdotal way, so that some of the things we did, so we did James Brown covers, we had a really good singer and dancer. And we played all over the Bay area from the most affluent University of California Law School reception, to a dance in the projects. And you’d do a dance in the projects and you’re up there on stage playing, and there’s 200 people, 200 kids in a line all doing the same dance coordinated together. And first of all you realize, oh, that’s what this music is about. It’s functional music. This was just — you know forget you on stage, that’s just a secondary

role. This is functional music, this is culture, this is social interrelationships. And to see that was just an eye opening experience for an 18-year-old kid who grew up in Jewish culture you know. It was fantastic. And I think there are many other anecdotal instant answers like that of just experiencing life in ways in which musics of African-American origin had a cultural meaning that I didn’t find elsewhere. It wasn’t a split between music and life. I think another component of the answer that can go down a rabbit hole is that in spite of what I said about innovators and imitators and my apprehensions about carrying that too far, I do believe in this idea there are people who came up with these ideas and if you were to ask me who I thought were the 50 most important jazz musicians, probably 48 of them would be black. I think I would probably throw Metheny and Stan Getz in there, and I don’t know who else.
